- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. - dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).

1	/**
2	 * Wear logging — the one write path every wear-derived surface reads from.
3	 *
4	 * Times worn, cost-per-wear, last worn, the Fit Diary grid, streaks, "most
5	 * worn" and "gathering dust" are all views over wear_logs. Nothing wrote to it
6	 * before this.
7	 */
8	
9	/** The button states itself: an instruction before, a fact after. */
10	export function wearLabel(worn: boolean): string {
11	  return worn ? "Worn today" : "Wear this today";
12	}
13	
14	/**
15	 * `worn_on` is a DATE column, compared against the user's LOCAL date key — a
16	 * UTC comparison would move an evening wear in an eastern timezone onto the
17	 * next day, which is the same class of bug the daily drop already avoids.
18	 */
19	export function isWornToday(logs: { worn_on: string }[], today: string): boolean {
20	  return logs.some((l) => l.worn_on === today);
21	}
22	
23	/**
24	 * Where a regenerated set starts numbering, given the indices already pinned.
25	 *
26	 * A worn outfit is pinned: `saveDailyLooks` leaves it out of the day's delete so
27	 * that wearing a look and then regenerating cannot destroy what you actually
28	 * wore (the FK had no ON DELETE action, so it used to fail outright). But
29	 * `outfits_daily_unique` is `(user_id, occasion, generated_on, look_index)`, so
30	 * the fresh set has to be numbered past the survivors.
31	 *
32	 * Indices only ever move forward — gaps left by a previous regenerate are not
33	 * reused, because reusing one would collide with a look pinned in between.
34	 */
35	export function freshIndexStart(pinned: (number | null)[]): number {
36	  const used = pinned.filter((i): i is number => typeof i === "number");
37	  return used.length === 0 ? 0 : Math.max(...used) + 1;
38	}

content.text:
The change adds three pure helper functions and their unit tests. Neither file is imported anywhere else in the repo yet (grep for `freshIndexStart|isWornToday|wearLabel` returns only these two files), so there is no source→sink path introduced by this diff.

Function-by-function:

- `wearLabel(worn: boolean)`: pure boolean → static string. No sink.
- `isWornToday(logs, today)`: string equality (`===`) over a caller-supplied array. No SQL/shell/eval/DOM/log sink; no injection surface.
- `freshIndexStart(pinned)`: filters to numbers, returns `Math.max(...used) + 1`. Pure arithmetic; the values come from the DB's `look_index` column (bounded by outfits-per-day per the accompanying comments), not attacker-controlled to a scale that would matter for the `Math.max` spread. No sink.

No parser differentials, no fail-open state, no gate/action mismatch, no registry fanout, no observability leak — the changes don't touch any of those surfaces. The functions are helpers that other code will consume later; when those call sites land they should be reviewed for how they build the `today` key and how they use `freshIndexStart`'s return in the DB insert, but that's out of scope for this diff.
